counterexample: Line 0015 claims H_1 \cap N_2 \lhd H_1. Take G = S_3, H_1 = S_3, H_2 = {e, (12)}, N_2 = {e, (12)} (so N_2 \lhd H_2 since H_2 is abelian), and N_1 = A_3 \lhd H_1 = S_3. Then H_1 \cap N_2 = {e, (12)}, which is NOT normal in H_1 = S_3: (13)(12)(13)^{-1} = (23) \notin {e, (12)}. The cited result 'Intersection with Normal Subgroup is Normal' needs N_2 \lhd G (or at least N_2 normal in a group containing H_1); here N_2 is only normal in H_2. The correct available facts are H_1 \cap N_2 \lhd H_1 \cap H_2 and H_2 \cap N_1 \lhd H_1 \cap H_2. (The theorem's conclusion is still true; the cited intermediate claims are not.)
reasoning_summary: 0001 OK: legitimate to take an arbitrary element of H_1 \cap H_2, the group in which normality is to be shown. 0003-0004 OK: definition of set intersection gives x_h \in H_1 and x_h \in H_2. 0006-0007 OK as a statement of the goal: setwise conjugation-invariance is the right target for a normality proof. 0009-0011 GAP: the Normal Subgroup Test requires (H_1 \cap N_2)(H_2 \cap N_1) to already be a subgroup of H_1 \cap H_2; the proof never checks that the product set is a subgroup, nor that it is contained in H_1 \cap H_2, so conjugation-invariance alone does not yield the stated conclusion (both facts are true but must be established, e.g. from product of two normal subgroups being a subgroup). 0013 FAILS as a citation: 'Intersection with Normal Subgroup is Normal' has hypothesis N \lhd G, H \le G, concluding H \cap N \lhd H; the hypotheses N_1 \lhd H_1 and N_2 \lhd H_2 do not supply normality in G, so the theorem is not applicable as invoked. 0015 FAILS (first failing step): 'H_1 \cap N_2 \lhd H_1' is false in general - see counterexample (G = S_3, H_1 = S_3, H_2 = N_2 = {e,(12)}); only H_1 \cap N_2 \lhd H_1 \cap H_2 follows. 0016 FAILS symmetrically: 'H_2 \cap N_1 \lhd H_2' is false in general by the mirrored counterexample (swap the roles of the pairs). 0018 OK: bare connective introducing the computation. 0021-0022 OK: inserting x_h^{-1} x_h = e between the two factors is a valid rewriting of the setwise conjugate. 0025-0026 OK: regrouping by associativity (Group Axiom 1). 0028-0029 OK: x_h^{-1} x_h = e by definition of inverse. 0031-0032 OK: e absorbed by the identity axiom - but note 0022-0031 is a closed loop that returns to the original expression, so these four steps are mathematically valid yet contribute nothing. 0034-0035 UNSOUND AS JUSTIFIED: the equality x_h (H_1 \cap N_2)(H_2 \cap N_1) x_h^{-1} = (H_1 \cap N_2) x_h (H_2 \cap N_1) x_h^{-1} needs x_h (H_1 \cap N_2) = (H_1 \cap N_2) x_h, and the stated warrant is the false line 0015; it is rescuable only via the corrected fact H_1 \cap N_2 \lhd H_1 \cap H_2 together with x_h \in H_1 \cap H_2. 0037-0038 UNSOUND AS JUSTIFIED for the same reason: x_h (H_2 \cap N_1) x_h^{-1} = H_2 \cap N_1 rests on the false line 0016, and is rescuable only via H_2 \cap N_1 \lhd H_1 \cap H_2. 0041 NOT ESTABLISHED: the QED rests on the two false normality claims plus the unverified subgroup hypothesis of the Normal Subgroup Test. Overall: the final statement is a true theorem and the algebraic manipulations are individually correct, but the proof as written asserts two false intermediate lemmas (0015, 0016) and omits the required subgroup check, so it does not verify.
